doc.title: Stefon Harris interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 11, 2020

title: Playing with the time and the black church
summary: Harris says Blackout does not chase odd meters, and relates time feel to growing up in the black church where his mother is a minister.

story.theme_name: Church, faith and religion in a musician's life
story.community_name: Church, faith and jazz: the sacred and the secular

blocks.x: Those are good questions. We’ve put some difficult inquiries to you today and I appreciate your thoughtfulness. We could wrap up shortly. There was one thing I wanted to get in, this is when I listened to your first selection on the preview I had this phrase that has been coming up. And it has to do mostly with current jazz or in the last let’s say twenty years. The difference between playing the time and playing with the time. Playing
with the time. And I guess I thought that for a while everybody in your group was playing with the time. Am I anywhere close to being with my observation —

Well no, no. It’s an interesting perspective that you’re bringing up because there is a significant faction of the young jazz world that is playing with the time, for the past two decades or whatever. You’ve had all these songs in 13-1/2 [over] 8 for fifty odd measures and performed this experiment, and there’s nothing wrong with that. But I think Blackout, our band, we don’t come from that perspective at all. If something ends up in an odd meter it’s because it revealed itself that way. It makes you always feel good — the way that I think time works for me is definitely with a cultural quality. My mother is a minister. I grew up in the black church. And I remember someone just standing up and just saying, you know “I want to thank you because last week you prayed for my brother and he was sick and I want to let you know he’s feeling better.” Bang, then the choir would come in just out of nowhere. And then they would start speaking but they would start using pitches, right? So [sings] “I just wanted to let you know” and the choir would come in. So all the phrasing was completely part of the whole, connected to authentic expression. Now was it right on the beat? Behind the beat? I don’t think that that’s relevant. What makes music feel good is first and foremost your internal coordination. So I could take any phrase, it doesn’t matter, and play it in the complete wrong spot, and if my internal coordination is strong enough it’s going to feel good. So it’s that kind of thing that is not an intentional, okay we’re going to try this complex pattern. Again, nothing wrong with that but that’s not where we were coming from. We’re really trying to testify from the heart of the spirit. And I think that’s what’s in the hearts and minds of our feelings.
